content.text: Based on the supplied RH134 course material (RH134) book, Chapter 1, pages 1–36.
The goal of this chapter is simple: learn how to make Linux perform repetitive tasks automatically, make decisions, and find important information quickly.
The book divides the chapter into three main topics:
Running Commands More Efficiently Using Loops
Matching Text in Command Output with Regular Expressions
We will follow this order, including the main concepts and practical examples. At the end, we will connect all three topics into one system administration task.
Topic 2: Running Commands More Efficiently Using Loops
Topic 3: Matching Text in Command Output with Regular Expressions

sections.title: 1.1 Creating and executing Bash shell scripts

content.text: Main idea: A Bash script is a text file containing commands that Linux can execute in sequence.
Simple explanation: Imagine checking a server manually every morning. You run lsblk, then df -h, then check other information. A script is like a checklist that performs these commands for you.
#!/bin/bash — tells Linux which command interpreter should run the script when it is executed directly.
date — displays the current date and time.
df -h — displays filesystem space in readable units, such as GB.
bash firstscript.sh — asks Bash to read and execute the commands in the file.
Linux runs the commands from top to bottom. You write the commands once and can run them whenever needed.
Remember: A script turns a list of commands into a reusable task.
Main idea: The first line tells Linux which interpreter should understand the script.
The book calls #! the shebang. Think of it as a label telling Linux which tool should read the instructions.
/bin/bash — the location of the Bash interpreter.
Without the correct interpreter, a script might not be processed as intended when executed directly.
Remember: The shebang identifies the interpreter for your script.
Main idea: To run a script directly like an ordinary command, it needs execute permission.
u+x — adds execute permission for the file's owner.
./ — tells Linux to look for the script in the current directory.
There are two common ways to run it:
The first explicitly starts Bash to read the file. The second executes the script directly, requiring suitable execute permission and a valid interpreter line.
The book also introduces PATH, the list of directories Bash searches when you type a command name.
echo "$PATH" — displays the directories in PATH.
which bash — shows the location of the Bash executable found through the command search path.
Remember: Use bash script.sh to run through Bash, or ./script.sh to execute the script directly.
Main idea: Quotes and backslashes help Bash understand whether a character is an instruction or ordinary text.
Bash gives special meaning to characters such as #, $, *, and ?. Sometimes you want to display those characters instead of letting Bash interpret them.
Think of quotation marks as putting a protective cover around text.
echo '# not a comment' displays # not a comment.
echo "My username is $USER" displays the value stored in USER.
Single quotes ' ' — preserve the enclosed text literally.
Double quotes " " — allow variable and command substitution but prevent many unwanted expansions.
Backslash \ — protects the special meaning of the character immediately after it.
$USER — accesses the value stored in the USER variable.
This displays $USER instead of your username.
Remember: Single quotes preserve text literally; double quotes allow variables to be expanded.

sections.title: 1.5 Providing output from a shell script

content.text: Main idea: A script can display messages, send errors separately, and save its output to files.
Imagine a server report with two types of information: normal results and error messages. Linux provides separate output channels for these.
echo "Server report" — sends normal output to standard output, called STDOUT.
>&2 — sends the error message to standard error, called STDERR.
2> — redirects standard error into a file.
The terminal displays Server report, while errors.log contains the error message.
The book also shows how to save normal output using > and add more output using >>.
> creates or overwrites the file; >> adds to the end.
Remember: STDOUT is for normal results, STDERR is for errors, and redirection controls where they go.
Main idea: A loop repeats commands for multiple items without requiring you to type the same command repeatedly.
Imagine checking the hostname of five servers. You could run the command five times, or give Bash a list of server names and let it repeat the task.
The book introduces the for loop.
for HOST in servera serverb serverc
HOST — a variable that temporarily holds one item.
in — introduces the list of items.
do — begins the commands to repeat.
done — marks the end of the loop.
Bash runs the commands once for each item. First, HOST contains servera, then serverb, then serverc.
Remember: A for loop takes a list, handles one item at a time, and repeats the same commands.
Main idea: A loop's list can be typed manually or generated by Bash.
The book demonstrates several ways to create lists.
for HOST in servera serverb serverc
$NUM — retrieves the current value of the variable.
The book also demonstrates filename expansion, such as file*, and command substitution, which uses the output of another command to generate list items.
Remember: You do not always need to type every list item manually; Bash can generate the list.

sections.title: 2.3 Using loops to check multiple servers

content.text: Main idea: Loops become especially useful when combined with real administration commands.
The book's guided exercise uses SSH to obtain hostnames from multiple servers.
HOST — holds the current server name.
ssh — connects to a remote server.
student@"$HOST" — connects as user student to the server stored in HOST.
hostname — asks the remote server to display its hostname.
Instead of manually connecting to each server and typing hostname, the loop handles both servers automatically.
The book then extends this idea by putting the loop inside a script, allowing you to reuse the same process later.
Remember: A loop combined with SSH can automate the same administrative check across many servers.
Main idea: An exit code tells you whether a command or script completed successfully.
Imagine a command returns a small result card after finishing: 0 means success, while a nonzero number indicates failure.
The first command lists /etc. If it succeeds, the second command normally displays:
The second command will display a nonzero exit code.
$? — contains the exit code of the most recently executed command.
exit 0 — ends a script and reports success.
exit 1 — ends a script and reports a failure status.
A critical detail: check $? immediately after the command you want to evaluate. Running another command first changes the value.
Remember: Exit code 0 means success; a nonzero exit code means something did not succeed.
Main idea: Tests let Bash compare values and determine whether a condition is true or false.
Imagine checking whether a disk has more than 10 GB of free space. Before deciding what to do, you need a way to compare values.
The book introduces Bash's test command and its bracket forms.
The test succeeds because 8 is greater than 2.
Important comparison operators from the book:
[ ... ] — asks Bash to evaluate a test.
Spaces inside the brackets are required.
Remember: A test evaluates a condition, and its exit code tells you whether the condition succeeded.
Main idea: An if statement allows a script to perform an action only when a condition succeeds.
Think of a security checkpoint: if your identification is valid, you enter; otherwise, you do not.
then — introduces the action to perform if the test succeeds.
fi — closes the if statement. It is if spelled backward.
The command inside the block runs because the condition is true. If the condition were false, Bash would skip the block.
The book applies this concept to system administration by checking whether a service is active before deciding whether to start it.
Remember: if checks a condition; then tells Bash what to do when it succeeds.
Main idea: else gives your script an alternative action when the condition fails.
echo "The number is not greater than 10"
The number is not greater than 10
then — defines the action when the condition is true.
else — defines the alternative action when it is false.
Only one branch runs. Since 8 is not greater than 10, Bash executes the else branch.
Remember: if/then/else lets a script choose between two paths.
Main idea: elif allows a script to check additional conditions before choosing a final alternative.
Imagine checking which database service is available. You might prefer MariaDB, use PostgreSQL if MariaDB is unavailable, and choose another option if neither is active.
Here, STATUS is a variable containing a value.
elif — checks another condition if the first fails.
Bash checks conditions in order and runs the first matching branch. It skips the remaining branches afterward.
Remember: Use elif when you need to choose among more than two possible outcomes.
Main idea: A regular expression is a pattern that describes the text you want to find.
Imagine searching a large book for every line containing the word cat. A regular expression tells Linux what pattern to look for.
grep — searches text for matching patterns.
The search matches cat wherever it appears in a line, including inside longer words.
Regular expressions are used by tools such as grep, vim, and less. They have their own symbols and rules for describing more specific patterns.
Remember: A regular expression describes what text to find; grep searches for it.

sections.title: 3.2 Matching the start and end of a line

content.text: Main idea: The ^ and $ symbols restrict a match to a particular position in a line.
Without these symbols, grep 'cat' matches cat anywhere in a line. Sometimes you only want lines that begin or end with particular text.
cat$ — matches lines ending with cat.
^ — marks the beginning of a line.
$ — marks the end of a line.
For example, ^cat matches category, because it begins with cat. It does not match concatenate, because that line begins with con.
Likewise, cat$ matches a line containing only cat, but not category.
Remember: ^ controls the beginning of a line; $ controls the end.
Main idea: Character patterns let you match more than one possible character at a position.
Square brackets [] define a set of characters that can match at that position.
This searches for cat or cot.
c — the first character must be c.
[ao] — the next character can be a or o.
t — the last character must be t.
Match a lowercase letter in the range
Match a character other than a, b, or c
The ^ symbol has a different meaning inside a character set when it appears immediately after [; there it means “not these characters.”
Remember: Square brackets describe which characters are allowed at a position.
Main idea: Regular-expression repetition symbols control how many times a pattern can appear.
Suppose you want to find words containing zero or more occurrences of a particular character. Instead of writing a separate pattern for every possible length, you can use repetition symbols.
This matches lines where a c is followed later by a t, with any characters in between, including none.
Zero or more occurrences of the preceding pattern
Exactly n occurrences in basic regular expressions
This matches lines containing exactly three digits, such as 123 or 007.
Remember: Repetition symbols let you describe how many times a character or pattern may occur.
Main idea: Character classes provide readable ways to describe groups of characters.
Instead of listing every possible digit or letter, you can use a named character class.
Whitespace, such as spaces and tabs
This displays lines containing at least one digit.
These classes are particularly useful when searching configuration files and logs containing usernames, IDs, numbers, or status messages.
Remember: Character classes describe groups of characters without requiring you to list them individually.
Main idea: grep applies your pattern to a file or to text received from another command.
You have already seen how grep searches for words and character patterns. The next step is to use it in everyday administration.
| — sends the output of the first command to the next command.
This is called a pipeline. Think of it as an assembly line: the first command produces information, and the second filters it.
Remember: grep searches text in files or filters the output of other commands.
Main idea: Options change which matching lines grep displays.
Show lines that do not match
Show a number of lines after a match
Show a number of lines before a match
Specify a pattern; multiple -e options can search for alternatives
Searches for error regardless of letter case.
Displays lines that do not match error.
Displays each matching line and two lines after it.
Remember: Learn the pattern first, then use options to control the results.

sections.title: 3.8 Searching command output and configuration files

content.text: Main idea: Combining pipes, patterns, and grep makes it easier to find important information in large amounts of output.
Imagine a server has hundreds of running processes. You do not need to read every line manually; you can filter the results.
systemctl list-units — lists systemd units currently loaded.
| — passes the output to the next command.
grep -i 'ssh' — shows lines containing ssh, without case sensitivity.
The same idea works with configuration files and logs. You can search for errors, service names, usernames, or specific settings.
The book recommends placing regular-expression patterns in single quotes because symbols such as $, *, and {} can otherwise be interpreted by Bash before grep receives them.
Remember: First generate the information, then filter it to find what matters.
Now let's connect all three topics into one practical example.
Imagine you are a Linux administrator responsible for checking two servers. You want to collect their hostnames, check whether a service is running, and search the results for a particular word.
Create a file containing the commands you want to run.
The script organizes the task into reusable instructions.
Repeat a check for multiple servers and make decisions based on the results.
The loop handles each server; conditions can decide what to do based on success or failure.
Filter output to find a particular service or error.
The pipeline passes the output to grep, which searches for matching lines.
These examples illustrate how the concepts fit together; they are not a complete production monitoring script. Remote service checks also depend on SSH access and suitable permissions.
Save a sequence of commands so you can reuse it.
Repeat actions for multiple items and choose what happens next.
Search files and command output for the information you need.
Remember this sequence: Automate → Repeat and decide → Search and filter.
That is the central idea of Chapter 1: making command-line administration more efficient, repeatable, and accurate.
Try answering these three questions in your own words:
1. What is the main purpose of a Bash script?
To store and run a sequence of commands
To create user accounts automatically in every case
2. What does a for loop do?
Searches a file for a word
Repeats commands for each item in a list
3. What is the relationship between grep and a regular expression?
They are exactly the same thing
grep creates files, while regular expressions delete them
grep searches text using a pattern that can be a regular expression
Once these ideas make sense, you have the foundation needed to understand the chapter's guided exercises and final lab.
